title: Ashura: two ways
hookLine: a Sunni fast and a Shia commemoration, each explained by its own people

lines: A HALL IN BLACK, A STORY RECITED.
cards: Same date, two rooms. In one kitchen, before dawn, a family eats quietly so they can fast through the day, thankful for a rescue in the time of Musa. Across town, people dressed in black fill a hall in the evening.
Someone recites, slowly, the story of a grandson of the Prophet and the thirst of his family, and people weep. At the door, volunteers hand out cups of water. Both are keeping Ashura.

teach.b: You met both ways back in year two; today, side by side. First, the fast, as Sunni Muslims explain it. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a report from Ibn 'Abbas.
When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Madinah, he found the Jews there fasting on the day of Ashura. He asked why.

They told him, in paraphrase: it's a good day, the day Allah saved the Children of Israel from their enemy, so Musa fasted it. He answered: I have more right to Musa than you. So he fasted it, and told people to fast.
In Sahih Muslim he says he hopes the fast of Ashura wipes away the sins of the year before, and in another report, that if he lives to the next year, he'll fast the ninth as well.
So some Sunni families fast the day before too. Second, the commemoration, as Shia Muslims explain it.

teach.h: A MOURNING FOR HUSAYN AT KARBALA.
teach.b: On Ashura, the histories say, Husayn ibn 'Ali, the Prophet's grandson, was killed at Karbala with members of his family and companions, after days cut off from water. For Shia Muslims, the day is one of mourning.
They gather in majalis, where the story is told and elegies are recited. In some places there are processions. Water is given out, in memory of the thirst at Karbala.
Shia speakers describe Husayn's stand as a refusal to bow to injustice, and grief for him as keeping faith with that stand. Third, these aren't strangers to each other's day.
Sunni tradition honors Husayn too: a hadith in al-Tirmidhi calls Hasan and Husayn the leaders of the youth of Paradise.
One date, two ways of keeping it, and each makes sense from inside.

how: Sunni practice includes a voluntary fast on Ashura, sometimes with the day before it, following hadiths in al-Bukhari and Muslim; Shia Muslims keep Ashura as a day of mourning for Husayn ibn 'Ali at Karbala, with gatherings called majalis, recited elegies, processions in some places, and the giving of water.

o: the feast that marks the end of the pilgrimage
a day in Muharram, kept with a fast and with mourning
the night in Ramadan when the Qur'an was first revealed

p: gatherings where the story is told
in memory of the thirst at Karbala

s: Ashura is kept the same way by every Muslim
Sunni practice includes a fast; Shia Muslims keep it as a day of mourning for Husayn.
in al-Bukhari, the Prophet found the Jews of Madinah fasting on Ashura
they told him it was the day Allah saved the Children of Israel, and Musa fasted it.
Sunni tradition honors him too; a hadith in al-Tirmidhi calls Hasan and Husayn leaders of the youth of Paradise.

games.q: the Prophet, newly arrived in Madinah, finds his Jewish neighbors fasting on Ashura. what does he do?
o: asks why, then fasts it himself and tells others to fast.
games.why: he asked, heard it was the day Allah saved the Children of Israel, said he had more right to Musa, and fasted it and told people to fast.

practice: Bring the two scenes to mind, the quiet kitchen before dawn and the hall with cups of water at the door, and spend a few breaths with each without choosing between them.
Then shape one curious, gentle question you might someday ask a neighbor about how their family keeps Ashura. If you pray, you can remember Musa's rescue and Husayn's family together.

wordCard.voice: Ashura. A day in Muharram, kept by Sunni Muslims with a fast for Musa's rescue, and by Shia Muslims as a day of mourning for Husayn at Karbala. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the day in Muharram.

carryVoice: Your line: two ways of keeping it. One date, two rooms, both keeping it. Tomorrow, Rabi' al-Awwal.
